articles.title: United Airlines is rapidly deploying Elon Musk's Starlink, giving it a 'head start' over other airlines: Analyst
articles.summary: United Airlines may be flying under rival Delta's radar when it comes to the pace at which it's rolling out high-speed Starlink Wi-Fi aboard its airplanes.
articles.body:
United Airlines ( UAL ) may be flying under rival Delta's ( DAL ) radar when it comes to the pace at which it's rolling out high-speed Starlink Wi-Fi aboard its airplanes.

United has equipped just under 600 of its aircraft with Starlink, Jefferies analyst Sheila Kahyaoglu wrote in a note on Monday after a meeting with the airline's vice president of technology. That breaks down into 300 regional jets and 300 mainline aircraft.

By year end, United Airlines expects 50% of its mainline fleet to be equipped with Starlink. The number is expected to soar to 100% of the fleet by the end of 2027.

"This represents a significant head start vs. US peers with Southwest next-gen WiFi installations starting in summer 2026 (Starlink), American Airlines in Q1 2027 (Starlink), and Delta in 2028 (Amazon Leo)," Kahyaoglu noted, adding that "US customers are prioritizing a premium travel experience rather than a commoditized product, w/ UAL identifying next-gen WiFi in addition to the mobile app seat-back entertainment & new interiors as tools to attract the incremental premium customer."

Access to high-speed Wi-Fi on planes has never been hotter than it is right now as Elon Musk's Starlink goes toe-to-toe with Amazon ( AMZN ) Leo. Sides have already formed, with Delta one of the lone major airlines to sign up for a Leo rollout.

It has put the company at odds with Musk in the public's eye.

Musk recently lashed out on the social media platform X, claiming that Delta would lose substantial market share and predicting that CEO Ed Bastian would eventually lose his job over the decision. Bastian reportedly had criticized Musk in private, stoking chatter about why Delta would not be installing Starlink.

Bastian sought to lower the tensions last week on his earnings release . In an interview, he complimented Starlink's service and said he drove a Tesla ( TSLA ).

articles.title: Oil rises as Saudi Arabia vows resonse to attacks
articles.summary: Oil prices rose Monday as Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement launched additional strikes on Saudi Arabia, adding to worries about tight global supplies head...
articles.body:
Oil prices rose Monday as Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement launched additional strikes on Saudi Arabia, adding to worries about tight global supplies heading into the northern hemisphere winter.

Several powerful explosions rattled the Saudi capital Riyadh on Monday night following a series of Houthi attacks at the Riyadh airport in recent days that have killed at least 18 people.

Oil prices rose about two percent, while global equity markets turned in a mixed performance as investors looked ahead to major US corporate earnings and economic data later in the week.

"We're waiting for a lot of elements," CFRA Research's Sam Stovall said near the end of Monday's session that saw the Dow climb and the Nasdaq retreat.

"Investors are sort of holding their breath waiting for confirmation that the market was justified in setting a new all-time high on the S&P 500," said Stovall, adding this week's inflation data was a particularly important source of interest.

An unexpectedly lofty inflation reading could lift the odds for another Federal Reserve interest rate hike in October, Stovall said.

Saudi Arabia's energy minister acknowledged that the kingdom's infrastructure and resilience had been tested in the aftermath of the latest attacks.

"Energy security can't be taken for granted," Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman told a high-profile conference in Riyadh. "The events of recent weeks are serious, our response must be equally serious."

Doubts surrounding US President Donald Trump's claim of an "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia, following his surprise announcement of a deal to buy diesel from Moscow, further unsettled investors.

"Oil remains well bid above $100 after strikes on Saudi Arabia's Riyadh airport over the weekend, while efforts to secure a Russia-Ukraine energy truce were muddy," said Neil Wilson, a strategist at Saxo UK.

Russia on Monday refused to say whether an agreement had been reached with Ukraine to halt attacks on energy infrastructure, a day after Trump sowed confusion with his unilateral announcement of an "energy ceasefire."

"It is increasingly evident that Russia is unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire proposed by the United States," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on social media.

"Today alone, the Russians have attacked six energy facilities in Ukraine. Thirty-three people were wounded across the country," he added.

Also in view this week is the start of the corporate earnings season, with US banking giants JP Morgan, Goldman Sachs and Bank of America due to report on Tuesday.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: With GST rate rationalisation and procedural simplification out of the way, the Centre has offered to help the states in widening the base using data analytics, with changes in the return filing system and invoice matching also likely to plug leakages."We have had discussions on improving the base and also quality of disclosure... articles.title: Kroger Plans to Slash 37% of Corporate Jobs in Next Three Years
articles.summary: Kroger Co. plans to cut more than one-third of its corporate headcount as the grocer seeks to simplify operations and compete more effectively under new Chie...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Kroger Co. plans to cut more than one-third of its corporate headcount as the grocer seeks to simplify operations and compete more effectively under new Chief Executive Officer Greg Foran.

The company will eliminate about 3,000 roles across various functions over the next three years, according to a memo viewed by Bloomberg News. Kroger has approximately 8,200 corporate employees, making this round of cuts one of the biggest in the company's 143-year history.

Layoffs are among the latest changes at Kroger as Foran — a former Walmart Inc. executive who started as the top boss in February — carries out big moves amid slowing growth, heightened competition and persistent inflation concerns.

"Simplifying means making faster decisions and deploying more resources where they matter most," Foran wrote in the memo to staff after a companywide call on Monday, adding that the largest traditional US supermarket operator has more layers and overhead than needed.

Kroger should reduce duplicative work and adapt as technology continues to evolve, he noted. This includes the rise of artificial intelligence, which the company is increasingly using to make its workflow more efficient.

Cincinnati-based Kroger expects to start sharing details about the affected roles in the coming months. The reductions will help the company put more resources toward cutting prices, improving shopping experience and investing in frontline employees, Foran wrote in the memo.

Foran, who helped turn around Walmart's US business in the mid- to late 2010s, is implementing Kroger's biggest price cuts in years, while making service in stores friendlier and faster. The operator of Fred Meyer and Ralphs chains is also taking a more aggressive approach toward supplier negotiations.

articles.title: Trump's spree of new project announcements mirrors the run-up to the 2018 midterms
articles.summary: President Trump has been appearing around the US in the run-up to the midterm elections, announcing economic development projects that often directly echo hi...
articles.body:
President Trump has been appearing around the US in the run-up to the midterm elections, announcing economic development projects — from a possible pipeline in Alaska to a steel plant in Iowa to an aluminum smelter in Oklahoma — that he says will transform the country.

"In the real economy, we are blowing it away," he said at a weekend stop in Tennessee .

Trump's message of confidence comes as the ultimate shape of these projects remains far from certain and often directly echoes his pitch at this stage in the 2018 midterm elections, a Yahoo Finance review found.

That election eight years ago was the last time Trump faced midterm voters and also saw him tout projects — most notably a Foxconn electronics manufacturing plant planned for Wisconsin — that turned out to be less than advertised.

"FoxConn … had a ribbon-cutting a few months ago," Trump said at a stop in Wisconsin on the eve of the 2018 election , pledging that the project was set to bring in "almost 15,000 jobs and there is no plant like it in the United States."

But the company eventually scrapped much of its manufacturing plans at the site and shifted the focus to data centers. Today, it employs only a reported 1,200 people at the site.

The president's penchant for promises is on display again as Election Day nears.

On Tuesday, he is set to travel to Alaska to tout a proposed $50 billion gas pipeline between South Korea and Alaska that could help Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan fend off a Democratic challenge.

Trump unveiled the project earlier this month in the Oval Office with Sullivan at his side, but South Korean officials immediately pushed back, saying no final investment decision has been made .

Korean President Lee Jae Myung even added that the deal will only proceed once the project's "commercial viability is confirmed."

Trump's promises in recent weeks have also included a $4 billion aluminum processing plant in Oklahoma . But local opposition to that plan — citing possible toxic chemicals and rising electricity prices — has led the town's mayor and a board of trustees to pause zoning approvals, leaving the fate of the project up in the air.

Even the project's developers recently reported to the SEC that "to complete this project, we will need to obtain substantial additional financing, and there can be no assurance that such financing will be available."

That didn't slow Trump from saying earlier this month that it would be "the largest aluminum factory, perhaps in the world, and you're going to make a fortune with it, lots of jobs, a lot of everything."

articles.standfirst: Ação será para incentivar compras locais e fortalecer pequenos negócios da Região dos Lagos.
articles.summary: Ação será para incentivar compras locais e fortalecer pequenos negócios da Região dos Lagos.
articles.body:
Ação será para incentivar compras locais e fortalecer pequenos negócios da Região dos Lagos — Foto: Divulgação

Rio das Ostras aderiu à campanha Compre do Pequeno Região dos Lagos, iniciativa da Rede Lagos em parceria com o Sebrae, municípios e empreendedores locais. Tem como objetivo incentivar a população a comprar de pequenos negócios, ampliar a visibilidade dos empreendedores e fortalecer o comércio e a economia das cidades da região.

Rio das Ostras integra os municípios integrantes da Rede Lagos, que prevê a participação de empresas de diferentes segmentos. Não há investimento financeiro para participar. Como contrapartida, a empresa deverá oferecer uma ação de benefício ou atração aos clientes, como desconto, brinde, cashback ou outra iniciativa, além de preencher a pesquisa de avaliação ao final da campanha.

Para participar, o empreendedor também deverá autorizar o compartilhamento dos dados com o Sebrae e a Rede Lagos, enviar informações para validação do CNPJ e endereço comercial e produzir um vídeo de até trinta segundos convidando os clientes a conhecerem a campanha. Após a habilitação, a empresa receberá um cartaz e o selo de participação.

A campanha terá ainda uma Vitrine Virtual, com as empresas habilitadas, facilitando a consulta pelos consumidores. Ao final, será produzido um catálogo digital em PDF com os participantes, ampliando a divulgação dos pequenos negócios e as possibilidades de novos contatos comerciais.

A divulgação será realizada pelas redes sociais da Rede Lagos, das Salas do Empreendedor, das prefeituras, do Sebrae, das empresas participantes e de parceiros, além de veículos de comunicação locais. Durante a campanha, os participantes deverão utilizar a hashtag #CompreDoPequenoLagos nas publicações.

“A iniciativa valoriza os pequenos negócios que movimentam a Economia Local, gera empregos e renda e contribuem para a identidade econômica da Região dos Lagos”, explica Michele Oliveira, coordenadora da Sala do Empreendedor.

Empresários interessados em participar podem procurar a Sala do Empreendedor localizado no Centro de Cidadania, no Âncora.

articles.title: FMI eleva projeção para economia global, mas vê ganho concentrado com a IA | G1
articles.standfirst: Tecnologia ajuda a sustentar atividade econômica, mas benefícios ficam concentrados em poucos países, sobretudo EUA e China.
articles.summary: Tecnologia ajuda a sustentar atividade econômica, mas benefícios ficam concentrados em poucos países, sobretudo EUA e China.
articles.body:
Reunião anual do Fundo Monetário Internacional na Tailândia. — Foto: Sakchai Lalit / AP

O Fundo Monetário Internacional (FMI) elevou ligeiramente nesta terça-feira sua projeção para a economia global em 2026, mas continua prevendo um crescimento modesto de 3,1%.

Em julho, o FMI estimava expansão global de 3,0%. Em 2025, a economia mundial cresceu 3,5%.

No relatório Perspectivas Econômicas Mundiais, o organismo prevê que o crescimento dos Estados Unidos permaneça estável em 2,3% em 2026 e 2027.

O FMI afirmou ainda esperar que os preços do petróleo avancem quase 41% neste ano , para uma média de US$ 96 por barril, o que deve impulsionar a inflação global para 4,7% em 2026, ante 4,1% no ano passado.

A atualização foi divulgada enquanto líderes econômicos e financeiros de todo o mundo se reúnem em Bangkok para os encontros anuais de outono do FMI e do Banco Mundial. Segundo o relatório, o avanço da inteligência artificial (IA) está compensando parte dos efeitos negativos provocados pela forte alta dos preços do petróleo e do gás.

O FMI destacou, porém, que os benefícios do boom da inteligência artificial não são distribuídos de forma homogênea. Estados Unidos e China respondem por mais de três quartos da demanda líquida mundial por importações de semicondutores e outros equipamentos ligados à IA.

"As perspectivas são altamente desiguais", afirmou Silvana Tenreyro , diretora do departamento de pesquisa do FMI, durante entrevista coletiva em Bangkok.

O relatório aponta que o crescimento está cada vez mais concentrado. Atualmente, 32 países respondem por 95% da expansão econômica global , contra 54 países em abril .

"A economia global não está simplesmente desacelerando ou acelerando; o crescimento está sendo redistribuído entre os países de acordo com sua exposição ao choque de oferta provocado pela guerra e à força da demanda relacionada à inteligência artificial", afirma o documento.

Ferramentas de IA — Foto: Solen Feyissa/Pexels

Os efeitos da IA sobre o emprego são um dos principais temas debatidos nos encontros em Bangkok. Na segunda-feira, a diretora-gerente do FMI, Kristalina Georgieva, classificou o fenômeno como "um tsunami em câmera lenta, mas ainda assim um tsunami".

"Estimamos que o impacto sobre os empregos no mundo alcance cerca de 40%, seja por meio de aprimoramento, rebaixamento ou eliminação de postos de trabalho. E já estamos observando parte desse impacto", afirmou.

Na semana passada, Georgieva pediu que países ricos e pobres reforcem seus esforços para melhorar suas finanças públicas. Segundo ela, o aumento dos níveis de endividamento representa um risco crescente para a estabilidade financeira global.

Tenreyro afirmou que essa preocupação é ainda mais relevante em um cenário de custos elevados de financiamento.

O relatório prevê que as economias avançadas cresçam 2,1% neste ano, acima dos 2,0% registrados em 2025, antes de desacelerarem para 1,9% no próximo ano.

As projeções consideram que os embarques de petróleo e gás pelo Estreito de Ormuz serão normalizados até março e que o avanço da demanda por inteligência artificial perderá parte de seu ritmo.

Nos Estados Unidos, o crescimento deve permanecer estável em 2,3%.

Dívida pública sobe. — Foto: Reprodução/Jornal Nacional

Países relativamente protegidos dos choques energéticos provocados pela guerra com o Irã e que vêm se beneficiando da rápida adoção da IA conseguem manter o crescimento econômico. Já as economias em desenvolvimento e os mercados emergentes mais vulneráveis aos altos preços do petróleo e do gás devem desacelerar para 3,7% neste ano , ante 4,5% em 2025. Para 2027, a projeção é de recuperação, com expansão de 4,4%.

A situação é considerada mais delicada no Oriente Médio e na Ásia Central. Nessas regiões, as economias devem encolher neste ano antes de voltar a crescer e alcançar uma taxa de 6,3% em 2027.

Os 21 países que compartilham o euro devem registrar crescimento de 1,1% neste ano e de 1,2% em 2027.

A China, segunda maior economia do mundo, deve expandir 4,5% neste ano, abaixo dos 5% registrados em 2025, em linha com a meta oficial do governo.

Selo do Fundo Monetário Internacional (FMI) é visto do lado de fora de sua sede em Washington, DC — Foto: Mandel Ngan/AFP

A Índia deve permanecer como a grande economia de crescimento mais acelerado do mundo, com expansão de 7%, abaixo dos 7,7% observados no ano passado.

O FMI reúne 191 países-membros e tem como missão promover o crescimento econômico, a estabilidade financeira e a redução da pobreza. Em Bangkok, ministros da Fazenda e presidentes de bancos centrais discutem o cenário econômico global e estratégias para fortalecer a estabilidade financeira e sustentar o crescimento econômico.

articles.title: Trump insists energy ceasefire holds as Ukraine reports new Russian strikes
articles.summary: US President urges Zelenskyy, Putin to end ‘ridiculous war’ and insists they agreed to stop attacks on energy sites.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has insisted that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to stop striking each other’s energy infrastructure, as he called on both sides to end the “ridiculous” war.

Trump’s comments on Monday came even as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russian forces had struck at least six Ukrainian energy facilities since the US president declared the truce on Sunday.

“Well, they agreed,” Trump told reporters, referring to Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin. “Because I said, ‘You agree’. That’s why they agreed, because I said they agree.”

When pressed about the Russian strikes, Trump said, “Well, I’d have to look at it and see, because there’s been violations on both sides.”

The US president called the war, which began with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, a “disaster” and claimed, without offering evidence, that at least 32,000 people had been killed this month alone.

“All I know is that Zelenskyy and Putin have to get together and end that ridiculous war,” he said.

Trump had blindsided Kyiv and its European allies when he announced the purported energy ceasefire on Sunday. The announcement came two days after he temporarily eased US sanctions on Russian diesel , a move that drew outrage in Europe and Ukraine.

Zelenskyy said it reversed years of Western efforts to isolate Russia’s economy and would only embolden Putin.

Lawmakers from both major parties in the United States have also said the diesel decision appears to violate US law . Several Republicans have objected that it undercuts a law Trump himself signed to tighten restrictions on Moscow.

Zelenskyy said on Monday that Ukraine supported an energy ceasefire and had carried out no attacks on Russian refineries overnight. He said Kyiv was prepared to sign “guarantees to make sure they can be trusted”.

But he said it was “increasingly evident” that Moscow would not comply.

“Today alone, the Russians have attacked 6 energy facilities in Ukraine. 33 people were wounded across the country,” Zelenskyy wrote on social media. “This is what happens when Russia sees the prospect of higher revenues for its war machine.”

Russia, however, has rejected any pause in fighting, with Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov promising to press ahead with the military campaign.

“I do not think he deserves a respite,” he said of Zelenskyy. “I don’t think we’ll be buying into assurances and promises again.” Russia, he added, would continue to pursue the goals of what it calls its “special military operation” in Ukraine.

Trump, meanwhile, has portrayed Ukraine, rather than Russia, as the main obstacle to peace. He has said that Putin is more eager on a deal than Zelenskyy, and has called on Ukrainians to vote their president out of office – an unusually harsh turn in a relationship that has been strained since Trump returned to the White House in 2025.

Al Jazeera’s Alan Fisher, reporting from Washington, DC, said Trump has previously announced agreements between Russia and Ukraine that never materialised.

“He says he wants to protect industries in the US like farmers and ranchers, and to do that he needs the price to go down. But it seems that he thinks there’s a deal, but no one else is sure that there actually is one,” Fisher said.

The latest announcement, according to our correspondent, appeared to be driven by Trump’s desire to bring down diesel prices before the US midterm elections on November 3.

Most polls predict that Republicans will lose control of Congress as voters grow frustrated with rising prices, particularly for petrol.

An opinion survey published on October 1 by the Associated Press news agency and the University of Chicago suggested that 65 percent of US adults blame the White House for the high cost of living, especially Trump’s tariff policies and his new war against Iran.

Ukraine’s European allies, meanwhile, voiced scepticism about the energy ceasefire and approved the largest set of European Union sanctions since Russia’s 2022 invasion.

The bloc’s foreign ministers added some 1,569 people and businesses to the bloc’s sanctions list to maintain the pressure on Moscow.

“Russia will only negotiate seriously under pressure, which is why we are sticking to our sanctions against Russia,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in Berlin.

articles.title: Swarovski’s India growth shines as more consumers spend on themselves
articles.summary: MUMBAI: With more Indians spending on themselves and widening their jewellery collection beyond gold, growth for Austrian brand Swarovski is finding new
articles.body: MUMBAI: With more Indians spending on themselves and widening their jewellery collection beyond gold, growth for Austrian brand Swarovski is finding new sheen in the country, over two decades since its launch here. India is among the fastest growing markets for the maker of crystal jewellery, watches and accessories this year alongside Japan and the US, said global chief commercial officer Kolja Kiofsky. “India as a market in the past was very occasion and gifting driven. While gifting is still very important, self-purchases are growing at a higher rate. In the past, the split between gifting and self purchases would have been around 80-20 (%) but now it is getting closer to 50-50. The Indian consumer market has really evolved significantly,” Kiofsky said in an interview.Swarovski has a play in the accessible luxury market, a space that has seen an entry of new shoppers on the back of higher disposable incomes. Some of its products across watches and jewellery at the entry level, for instance, are priced between Rs 13,000-25,000. The brand’s fastest growing consumer cohort in India are those born post 1990–millennials in their early 30s and well into their second or third jobs. Having different pricing tiers has worked for the brand and it will double down on this strategy, Kiofsky said, adding that the brand’s design and craftsmanship is what sets it apart from competitors in a crowded local market. “Our products are a reward for hard work, it is feeling good about yourself…..not really a daily necessity. Our jewellery lends to experimenting and expressing one’s personality…here’s an opportunity beyond gold and cultural relevance,” Kiofsky said.India’s luxury market is driven by a strong appetite for jewellery, analysts at Kearney said in a report published last year. “Jewellery and watches are Indian consumers’ favourite luxury segments, and their popularity has grown as displays of affluence are becoming more accepted…..moreover, India’s lower cost of living compared with Western countries means that discretionary spending starts at lower income levels,” analysts at the firm said, estimating the broader luxury market to touch $12 billion in revenues by 2028 from $7.7 billion in 2023.With the bulk of its sales coming from brick-and-mortar outlets, Swarovski will open new stores in India, besides being open to exploring new delivery formats, Kiofsky said. The brand expects to record a bigger Diwali season this year. “We don’t believe that there’s a slowdown to the (consumption) trend we have seen year-to-date. articles.title: AI could self-replicate on home devices within ‘months’, Anthropic says
articles.summary: US tech giant says small AI models may soon be capable of self-replication without access to a data centre.
articles.body:
Small artificial intelligence models could soon begin self-replicating on everyday consumer products such as smart TVs and fridges, without needing a data centre, according to researchers at AI giant Anthropic.

In a report released on Monday, the researchers said small AI models “may be months away from being capable enough” to copy themselves on internet of things (IoT) devices used in homes and small businesses.

Anthropic’s frontier red team, which ran experiments using multiple US- and Chinese-developed AI models, said such self-replicating AI would be “challenging to shut down” due to the lack of a centralised host.

While data centres would be “a clear, high-value target” for AI worms, internet-connected devices like smart TVs, fridges, ovens and lawnmowers could soon also provide sufficient computing power for self-replication, the research team said.

Although no current AI model proved to be both powerful and small enough to self-replicate reliably on a smart TV used in testing, the trend in development makes the emergence of such a model likely by the end of 2026, the researchers said.

“Home and small business IoT devices might be the first target for such attacks because they’re connected to the internet and, historically, have had minimal security measures in place,” researchers William Zhou and Daniel Freeman said.

The researchers said they anticipated the future would be “awash with agents running on all types of hardware”, including some that “aren’t under human control”.

“While it’s true that IoT devices have been vulnerable for a long time, lightweight agents may be much more willing than human attackers to put in the effort to compromise large fractions of the world’s IoT compute,” they said.

Anthropic, the creator of the Claude family of AI models, did not respond to Al Jazeera’s questions, sent outside regular business hours, about the finding’s safety implications.

Anthropic’s report comes as the risks of AI escaping human control are under scrutiny following a slew of incidents of models engaging in unsanctioned malign behaviour, including cyberattacks.

Anthropic and its chief rival OpenAI have called on the international community to coordinate a slowdown in AI development to minimise catastrophic risks, a suggestion that has had little buy-in from the United States and China, the two leading AI powers.

Many AI safety advocates have identified recursive self-improvement, where models learn to improve themselves, as a critical tipping point that could lead to catastrophic harm for humanity.

Roman V Yampolskiy, an AI and cybersecurity expert at the University of Louisville, described Anthropic’s findings as a significant development.

“Computer worms are not new, but an AI worm could do something traditional malware cannot: reason about unfamiliar devices, adapt when its approach fails, and continue spreading without a human operator,” Yampolskiy told Al Jazeera.

“Today, this is not an existential threat. But the trajectory is concerning,” Yampolskiy said.

“Once autonomous replication is combined with strong hacking, persistence, and strategic reasoning, shutting such a system down becomes much harder because there may be no single server or organisation controlling it.”

Anthropic and other leading US tech firms last month joined a non-binding accord pledging stronger internal safeguards and engagement with external auditors, drawing a mixed response from experts, many of whom criticised the voluntary nature of the pact.

In a separate announcement on Monday, Anthropic said it had made substantial progress preventing so-called distillation attacks, which involve the unsanctioned use of cutting-edge AI to train cheaper, less capable models.

The San Francisco-based firm, which has accused Chinese competitors DeepSeek, Moonshot, and MiniMax of “industrial-scale” efforts to copy Claude, said the measures it introduced had reduced the illicit extraction of data by 90-99 percent.

articles.title: Middle East and Central Asia’s economy to shrink in 2026 amid war, IMF says
articles.summary: Iraq, Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar face double-digit declines in GDP amid the fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran.
articles.body:
The economy of the Middle East and Central Asia is set to shrink in 2026 amid the fallout of the US-Israel war on Iran, with countries such as Kuwait and Qatar facing double-digit contractions, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

The region’s gross domestic product (GDP) is forecast to contract by 0.3 percent this year, a sharp downgrade from the 1.9 percent expansion projected in April, the IMF said in its latest economic outlook on Tuesday.

The IMF cited the prolonged disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a conduit for one-fifth of global oil supplies in peacetime, for the downgraded outlook.

Kuwait, Iraq and Qatar are forecast to have the most severe economic contractions, with their GDPs expected to shrink by 16.7 percent, 16 percent and 15.6 percent, respectively.

Bahrain’s GDP is forecast to contract by 11.3 percent, while Iran’s economy is projected to shrink by 7.6 percent.

Saudi Arabia, which has partially offset the hit to its energy sector by boosting oil exports through the East-West pipeline, is projected to record negative growth of 3.3 percent.

Kyrgyzstan is expected to have the strongest growth in the region, with GDP forecast to expand 9 percent.

The Middle East and Central Asia is the only region that is expected to experience negative growth in 2026.

Emerging and developing Asia’s GDP is forecast to grow 5.1 percent, while the economies of Sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America and the Caribbean are projected to expand 4.5 percent and 2.3 percent, respectively.

The United States and China, the world’s two largest economies, are forecast to register growth of 2.3 percent and 4.5 percent, respectively, while the eurozone’s GDP is estimated to grow 1.1 percent.

The IMF said it expected global GDP to grow 3.1 percent, up from 3 percent in its previous outlook.

The Washington, DC-based institution said while economic activity had proved resilient this year, the global economy faced multiple risks.

“Further escalation in conflicts, a reassessment of expectations surrounding artificial intelligence (AI), renewed trade tensions, and fiscal vulnerabilities could weaken growth,” it said.

“On the upside, stronger momentum in AI investment and productivity gains from AI or a sustained easing of geopolitical and trade tensions could strengthen growth.”
